On the rename — yes, but let's be honest about the tradeoff. Renaming means new npm name, new GitHub repo, new domain, all the fox-agent/fox/foxc strings in code and docs — real churn. It's only worth it if the new name is clearly better and cheaper to own.

 

The fox-agent.* domains at ~$12/yr are already cheap. The pain is that shorter fox domains are gone or hundreds/yr. So a rename only pays off if the new name has an affordable, available short domain.

 

Here are directions that tend to be cheap and available, grouped:

 

Keep it an animal/agent theme (on-brand, fox-adjacent):

- ferret — short, memorable, agent-y (ferrets "fetch" things). ferret.dev/ferret.run likely affordable.

- marten / sable / stoat — mustelids like a fox, obscure enough to be cheap and available.

- cub / kit — fox offspring, very short. kit.run, kitagent.dev.

 

Abstract / coined (almost always available + cheap):

- vulpine (fox-like, latin root) — vulpine.dev.

- tods / tod (a male fox) — tod.run, very short.

- renard (french for fox) — renard.dev.

- kettu (finnish fox) — short, available.

 

Functional/dev-signal names:

- agentloop / loopkit — describes what it is.

- ctxwork / ctxagent — leans into the context-surgery feature.

 

My honest recommendation: the fox-agent.dev/foxagent.dev pair at ~$24/yr total is already reasonable, and renaming a working project has real cost (npm, repo, docs, muscle memory). I'd only rename if you find a name you love with a cheap short domain. Of the above, vulpine.dev or ferret.dev are the strongest — on-brand (fox meaning), likely available, short enough.

 

But given "don't have much money": $24/yr for both fox domains is hard to beat, and the rename churn is a hidden cost. My lean is keep fox-agent, buy the two cheap .devs, and don't reopen the name.

=== mcpServers config ===

127: mcpServers: Record<string, McpServerConfig>;

189: * Every other extension point here — [mcpServers.*], [agents.*], [lsp.*]

216: * executable sections ([mcpServers.], [agents.], [lsp.], [providers.])

273: mcpServers: {},

420: "requestTimeoutMs", "diagnostics", "mcpServers", "agents", "lsp", "plugins",

512: if (t.mcpServers && typeof t.mcpServers === "object") {

514: const n = Object.keys(t.mcpServers as Record<string, unknown>).length;

515: if (n) cfg.warnings.push(project config: ${n} [mcpServers.*] entr${n === 1 ? "y" : "ies"} ignored in untrusted directory — trust this folder to enable);

=== buildRegistry mcp ===

setOutputCap(cfg.toolOutputCap ?? 30_000);

// ?? [] on both: Config is public surface an embedder (or a test) may build

// by hand, and a config written before these fields existed must degrade to

// "no warnings, no plugins" rather than crash the registry build.

const warnings: string[] = [...(cfg.warnings ?? [])];

const disabled = cfg.disabledPlugins ?? [];

 

// User plugins load before anything connects: a plugin may pack MCP servers

// and delegation targets alongside its tools, and those merge before

// mcpTools dials out. Bundled plugins first, through the exact merge path

// user plugins take.

const { effectiveConfigPath } = await import("../core/config.ts");

const { dirname } = await import("node:path");

const res = await loadPlugins(cfg.plugins ?? [], dirname(effectiveConfigPath()), disabled);

warnings.push(...res.warnings);

const plugins: FoxPlugin[] = [

...bundledPlugins().filter((p) => !bundledDisabled(p.name, disabled)),

...bundledProviderPlugins(),

...res.plugins,

];

 

// Integration packs: plugin-contributed servers merge under explicit config —

// a config file names what the user chose, a pack only suggests. Collisions

// are reported, never silent.

const packedServers = new Map<string, string>(); // server name -> plugin name

for (const p of res.plugins) {

for (const [name, s] of Object.entries(p.mcpServers ?? {})) {

if (!s || typeof s !== "object" || typeof (s as { command?: unknown }).command !== "string") continue;

if (!packedServers.has(name)) packedServers.set(name, p.name);

}

}

const servers: Record<string, McpServerConfig> = {};

for (const [name, pluginName] of packedServers) {

const pack = res.plugins.find((p) => p.name === pluginName)!;

servers[name] = (pack.mcpServers as Record<string, McpServerConfig>)[name];

}

for (const [name, s] of Object.entries(cfg.mcpServers ?? {})) {

if (packedServers.has(name)) warnings.push(mcp server '${name}' is configured explicitly — plugin-packed server ignored);

servers[name] = s;

}

 

// Same merge for delegation targets (ACP command or A2A url entries).

// Returned for the turn loop: task reads the merged table, so a packed

// remote agent is delegable with no config file.

const agents: Record<string, ExternalAgentConfig> = {};

for (const p of res.plugins) {

for (const [name, a] of Object.entries(p.agents ?? {})) {

if (!a || typeof a !== "object") continue;

// "default" is fox-agent delegating to itself and is synthesized at call

// time, so it is not a name a plugin may rebind either

if (name === "default") {

warnings.push(plugin '${p.name}' agent 'default' ignored — that name is fox-agent itself);

continue;

}

if (agents[name]) continue; // first pack wins; reported below at the collision site

agents[name] = a as ExternalAgentConfig;

}

}

for (const [name, a] of Object.entries(cfg.agents ?? {})) {

if (agents[name]) warnings.push(agent '${name}' is configured explicitly — plugin-packed agent ignored);

agents[name] = a;

}

 

// MCP enters the registry as the bundled:mcp plugin — same merge path and

// override warnings as every other tool source, and disabledPlugins

// switches the whole bridge off. First in the list: least specific wins.

const mcpPlugin: FoxPlugin = { name: "bundled:mcp", tools: [] };

if (bundledDisabled("mcp", disabled)) {

closeMcp(); // an earlier config may have connected; detached reap, don't leak the children

} else {

const mc = await mcpTools(servers);

warnings.push(...mc.warnings);

mcpPlugin.tools = [...mc.tools.values()];

}

plugins.unshift(mcpPlugin);

[453]agent

Filed: https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/45034. Now the three answers.

 

1. GH issue — done

Bun TOML parser: confusing error on invalid escape (Windows paths / regex), with a suggested clearer message + lenient-mode request. Noted in the file.

 

2. How to do highlighting properly

 

The current bug is a capital-letter heuristic + a cross-language keyword union. The right fix depends on how correct you want to be vs. dependency weight:

 

Option A — minimal patch (no new dep). In src/tui/highlight.ts:

- Only apply the "capitalized → type/class" tint when the fence language is a real code language (not text, md, or prose). Pass the lang into the capital-letter branch.

- Split the monolithic KEYWORDS set per-language family, or drop ambiguous short words (in, is, by, this, self) that collide with English prose. Keep only unambiguous keywords (const, function, return).

- Cheap, keeps the zero-dep frame-loop property, fixes the quote/prose highlighting you saw.

 

Option B — real grammar lib (Shiki / highlight.js). These build a real syntax tree, so they know In at a sentence start isn't the JS in. But:

- They're heavy (WASM grammars / large JS), and fox-agent re-renders per frame.

- You'd pre-tokenize each fence block once (not per frame) and cache the segments. Doable but a real integration.

- highlight.js has a small core + per-language modules you can tree-shake to just the languages you care about; that's the lighter of the two.

 

My recommendation: Option A. The prose-in-quotes case is the only one you actually hit, and a targeted patch fixes it without adding a dependency or per-frame cost. A grammar lib is overkill for a chat TUI and fights the existing line-local design. I can do Option A now — it's ~10 lines in highlight.ts.

 

3. Move ACP/A2A out of core into bundled plugins?

 

*Short answer: ACP client* and A2A client — yes, cleanly. ACP server — no, that one stays.**

 

Here's the coupling I found:

 

│ piece │ couples to │ movable? │

├──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────┤

│ ACP client (acp/client.ts, │ only task.ts lazy-imports it │ ✅ easy — wrap in a bundled │

│ 193 LOC) │ (runAcpAgent) │ plugin providing the task │

│ │ │ delegation │

│ A2A client (a2a/client.ts, │ only task.ts lazy-imports it │ ✅ easy — same │

│ 270 LOC) │ (runA2aAgent) │ │

│ ACP server (acp/server.ts, │ cli.ts spawns it directly on │ ❌ hard — it's an entrypoint, │

│ 325 LOC) │ --acp/fox acp; the whole │ not a tool; a plugin can't │

│ │ point is a stdio protocol │ own "spawn me on a CLI flag" │

│ │ server with pure stdout │ without a core hook │

 

The task tool is the natural seam. default (delegate to another fox) and url (A2A) are already resolved at call time. So you could make task itself a bundled plugin whose tools resolve delegation targets from config [agents.*], and move the ACP/A2A client code behind it. That drops @agentclientprotocol/sdk from the TUI startup path (it's already lazy-imported) and makes A2A purely opt-in.

 

The catch on the ACP server: fox --acp is a CLI subcommand that must speak pure stdio. A plugin model doesn't naturally own "be a stdio server process." You'd need a core mechanism to let a plugin register a protocol-server mode, which is more machinery than the 325 LOC it saves. Keep the ACP server in core.

 

Recommendation:

- Move A2A client + ACP client behind the task tool as a bundled plugin (bundled:delegate or similar). Removes the delegation clients from core, keeps task working.

- Keep ACP server in core (it's an entrypoint).

 

Want me to start with the highlight fix (Option A) and the MCP collapse, and treat the ACP/A2A client extraction as a follow-up? The MCP collapse is the biggest — I'd do that first if you want it this session.

export function highlightLine(line: string, lang: string): Seg[] {

const style = commentStyle(lang);

const segs: Seg[] = [];

let i = 0;

TOKEN.lastIndex = 0;

let m: RegExpExecArray | null;

while ((m = TOKEN.exec(line))) {

if (m.index > i) segs.push({ t: line.slice(i, m.index) });

const tok = m[0];

const isCommentTok = m[1] !== undefined;

if (isCommentTok) {

// only treat it as a comment when this language uses that introducer

if (style.line && style.line.test(tok)) segs.push({ t: tok, fg: R.COM, italic: true });

else segs.push({ t: tok });

} else if (m[2] !== undefined) segs.push({ t: tok, fg: R.STR });

else if (m[3] !== undefined) segs.push({ t: tok, fg: R.NUM });

else if (m[4] !== undefined) {

const isType = /^[A-Z]/.test(tok) && tok.length > 1;

if (KEYWORDS.has(tok)) segs.push({ t: tok, fg: R.KW, bold: isType });

else if (isType) segs.push({ t: tok, fg: R.NUM });

else segs.push({ t: tok });

}

i = TOKEN.lastIndex;

}

if (i < line.length) segs.push({ t: line.slice(i) });

return segs.length ? segs : [{ t: line }];

}

 

/**

* Diff coloring for a tool-output line: unified-diff and git-style markers get

* their own colors, everything else stays plain. Returns null for plain lines.

*/

export function diffSegs(line: string): Seg[] | null {

if (/^\+(?!\+\+)|^!/.test(line)) return [{ t: line, fg: R.DADD }];

if (/^-(?!---)|^</.test(line)) return [{ t: line, fg: R.DDEL }];

if (/^@@|^diff |^index |^--- |^\+\+\+ |^=+$/.test(line)) return [{ t: line, fg: R.DHUNK }];

if (/^\+\+\+ |^--- /.test(line)) return [{ t: line, fg: R.DHUNK }];

return null;

}

Published on 12/18/2025 – Text version

 

 

TOML v1.1.0

 

Tom's Obvious, Minimal Language.

 

By Tom Preston-Werner, Pradyun Gedam, et al.

 

Objectives

 

 

TOML aims to be a minimal configuration file format that's easy to read due to

obvious semantics. TOML is designed to map unambiguously to a hash table. TOML

should be easy to parse into data structures in a wide variety of languages.

 

Preliminaries

 

 

TOML is case-sensitive.

 

Whitespace means tab (U+0009) or space (U+0020).

 

Newline means LF (U+000A) or CRLF (U+000D U+000A).

 

A TOML file must be a valid UTF-8 encoded Unicode document.

 

Specifically this means that a file as a whole must form a

well-formed code-unit sequence.

Otherwise, it must be rejected (preferably) or have ill-formed byte sequences

replaced with U+FFFD, as per the Unicode specification.

 

Comment

 

 

A hash symbol marks the rest of the line as a comment, except when inside a

string.

 

This is a full-line comment

key = "value" # This is a comment at the end of a line

another = "# This is not a comment"

 

Control characters other than tab (U+0000 to U+0008, U+000A to U+001F, U+007F)

are not permitted in comments.

 

Comments should be used to communicate between the human readers of a file.

Parsers must not modify keys or values, based on the presence (or contents) of a

comment.

 

Key/Value Pair

 

 

The primary building block of a TOML document is the key/value pair.

 

Keys are on the left of the equals sign and values are on the right. Whitespace

is ignored around key names and values. The key, equals sign, and value must be

on the same line (though some values can be broken over multiple lines).

 

key = "value"

 

Values must have one of the following types.

 

String

 

Integer

 

Float

 

Boolean

 

Offset Date-Time

 

Local Date-Time

 

Local Date

 

Local Time

 

Array

 

Inline Table

 

Unspecified values are invalid.

 

key = # INVALID

 

There must be a newline (or EOF) after a key/value pair. (See

Inline Table for exceptions.)

 

first = "Tom" last = "Preston-Werner" # INVALID

 

Keys

 

 

A key may be either bare, quoted, or dotted.

 

Bare keys may only contain ASCII letters, ASCII digits, underscores, and

dashes (A-Za-z0-9_-). Note that bare keys are allowed to be composed of only

ASCII digits, e.g. 1234, but are always interpreted as strings.

 

key = "value"

bare_key = "value"

bare-key = "value"

1234 = "value"

 

Quoted keys follow the exact same rules as either basic strings or literal

strings and allow you to use a much broader set of key names. Best practice is

to use bare keys except when absolutely necessary.

 

"127.0.0.1" = "value"

"character encoding" = "value"

"ʎǝʞ" = "value"

'key2' = "value"

'quoted "value"' = "value"

 

A bare key must be non-empty, but an empty quoted key is allowed (though

discouraged). You cannot use multi-line strings to define quoted keys.

 

= "no key name" # INVALID

"""key""" = "not allowed" # INVALID

"" = "blank" # VALID but discouraged

'' = 'blank' # VALID but discouraged

 

Dotted keys are a sequence of bare or quoted keys joined with a dot. This

allows for grouping similar properties together:

 

name = "Orange"

physical.color = "orange"

physical.shape = "round"

site."google.com" = true

 

In JSON land, that would give you the following structure:

 

{

"name": "Orange",

"physical": {

"color": "orange",

"shape": "round"

},

"site": {

"google.com": true

}

}

 

For details regarding the tables that dotted keys define, refer to the

Table section below.

 

Whitespace around dot-separated parts is ignored. However, best practice is to

not use any extraneous whitespace.

 

fruit.name = "banana" # this is best practice

fruit. color = "yellow" # same as fruit.color

fruit . flavor = "banana" # same as fruit.flavor

 

Indentation is treated as whitespace and ignored.

 

Defining a key multiple times is invalid.

 

DO NOT DO THIS

name = "Tom"

name = "Pradyun"

 

Note that bare keys and quoted keys are equivalent:

 

THIS WILL NOT WORK

spelling = "favorite"

"spelling" = "favourite"

 

As long as a key hasn't been directly defined, you may still write to it and to

names within it.

 

This makes the key "fruit" into a table.

fruit.apple.smooth = true

 

So then you can add to the table "fruit" like so:

fruit.orange = 2

 

THE FOLLOWING IS INVALID

 

This defines the value of fruit.apple to be an integer.

fruit.apple = 1

 

But then this treats fruit.apple like it's a table.

You can't turn an integer into a table.

fruit.apple.smooth = true

 

Defining dotted keys out-of-order is discouraged.

 

VALID BUT DISCOURAGED

 

apple.type = "fruit"

orange.type = "fruit"

 

apple.skin = "thin"

orange.skin = "thick"

 

apple.color = "red"

orange.color = "orange"

 

RECOMMENDED

 

apple.type = "fruit"

apple.skin = "thin"

apple.color = "red"

 

orange.type = "fruit"

orange.skin = "thick"

orange.color = "orange"

 

Since bare keys can be composed of only ASCII integers, it is possible to write

dotted keys that look like floats but are 2-part dotted keys. Don't do this

unless you have a good reason to (you probably don't).

 

3.14159 = "pi"

 

The above TOML maps to the following JSON.

 

{ "3": { "14159": "pi" } }

 

String

 

 

There are four ways to express strings: basic, multi-line basic, literal, and

multi-line literal. All strings must contain only Unicode characters.

 

Basic strings are surrounded by quotation marks ("). Any Unicode character

may be used except those that must be escaped: quotation mark, backslash, and

the control characters other than tab (U+0000 to U+0008, U+000A to U+001F,

U+007F).

 

str = "I'm a string. \"You can quote me\". Name\tJos\xE9\nLocation\tSF."

 

For convenience, some popular characters have a compact escape sequence.

 

\b - backspace (U+0008)

\t - tab (U+0009)

\n - linefeed (U+000A)

\f - form feed (U+000C)

\r - carriage return (U+000D)

\e - escape (U+001B)

\" - quote (U+0022)

\\ - backslash (U+005C)

\xHH - unicode (U+00HH)

\uHHHH - unicode (U+HHHH)

\UHHHHHHHH - unicode (U+HHHHHHHH)

 

Any Unicode character may be escaped with the \xHH, \uHHHH, or \UHHHHHHHH

forms. The escape codes must be Unicode

scalar values.

 

Keep in mind that all TOML strings are sequences of Unicode characters, not

byte sequences. For binary data, avoid using these escape codes. Instead,

external binary-to-text encoding strategies, like hexadecimal sequences or

Base64, are recommended for converting between

bytes and strings.

 

All other escape sequences not listed above are reserved; if they are used, TOML

should produce an error.

 

Sometimes you need to express passages of text (e.g. translation files) or would

like to break up a very long string into multiple lines. TOML makes this easy.

 

Multi-line basic strings are surrounded by three quotation marks on each

side and allow newlines. A newline immediately following the opening delimiter

will be trimmed. All other whitespace and newline characters remain intact.

 

str1 = """

Roses are red

Violets are blue"""

 

TOML parsers should feel free to normalize newline to whatever makes sense for

their platform.

 

On a Unix system, the above multi-line string will most likely be the same as:

str2 = "Roses are red\nViolets are blue"

 

On a Windows system, it will most likely be equivalent to:

str3 = "Roses are red\r\nViolets are blue"

 

For writing long strings without introducing extraneous whitespace, use a "line

ending backslash". When the last non-whitespace character on a line is an

unescaped \, it will be trimmed along with all whitespace (including newlines)

up to the next non-whitespace character or closing delimiter. All of the escape

sequences that are valid for basic strings are also valid for multi-line basic

strings.

 

The following strings are byte-for-byte equivalent:

str1 = "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog."

 

str2 = """

The quick brown \

 

fox jumps over \

the lazy dog."""

 

str3 = """\

The quick brown \

fox jumps over \

the lazy dog.\

"""

 

Any Unicode character may be used except those that must be escaped: backslash

and the control characters other than tab, line feed, and carriage return

(U+0000 to U+0008, U+000B, U+000C, U+000E to U+001F, U+007F). Carriage returns

(U+000D) are only allowed as part of a newline sequence.

 

You can write a quotation mark, or two adjacent quotation marks, anywhere inside

a multi-line basic string. They can also be written just inside the delimiters.

 

str4 = """Here are two quotation marks: "". Simple enough."""

str5 = """Here are three quotation marks: """.""" # INVALID

str5 = """Here are three quotation marks: ""\"."""

str6 = """Here are fifteen quotation marks: ""\"""\"""\"""\"""\"."""

 

"This," she said, "is just a pointless statement."

str7 = """"This," she said, "is just a pointless statement.""""

 

If you're a frequent specifier of Windows paths or regular expressions, then

having to escape backslashes quickly becomes tedious and error-prone. To help,

TOML supports literal strings which do not allow escaping at all.

 

Literal strings are surrounded by single quotes. Like basic strings, they

must appear on a single line:

 

What you see is what you get.

winpath = 'C:\Users\nodejs\templates'

winpath2 = '\\ServerX\admin$\system32\'

quoted = 'Tom "Dubs" Preston-Werner'

regex = '<\i\c\s>'

 

Since there is no escaping, there is no way to write a single quote inside a

literal string enclosed by single quotes. Luckily, TOML supports a multi-line

version of literal strings that solves this problem.

 

Multi-line literal strings are surrounded by three single quotes on each

side and allow newlines. Like literal strings, there is no escaping whatsoever.

A newline immediately following the opening delimiter will be trimmed. TOML

parsers must normalize newlines in the same manner as multi-line basic strings.

 

All other content between the delimiters is interpreted as-is without

modification.

 

regex2 = '''I [dw]on't need \d{2} apples'''

lines = '''

The first newline is

trimmed in literal strings.

All other whitespace

is preserved.

'''

 

You can write 1 or 2 single quotes anywhere within a multi-line literal string,

but sequences of three or more single quotes are not permitted.

 

quot15 = '''Here are fifteen quotation marks: """""""""""""""'''

 

apos15 = '''Here are fifteen apostrophes: '''''''''''''''''' # INVALID

apos15 = "Here are fifteen apostrophes: '''''''''''''''"

 

'That,' she said, 'is still pointless.'

str = ''''That,' she said, 'is still pointless.''''

 

Control characters other than tab are not permitted in a literal string.

 

Integer

 

 

Integers are whole numbers. Positive numbers may be prefixed with a plus sign.

Negative numbers are prefixed with a minus sign.

 

int1 = +99

int2 = 42

int3 = 0

int4 = -17

 

For large numbers, you may use underscores between digits to enhance

readability. Each underscore must be surrounded by at least one digit on each

side.

 

int5 = 1_000

int6 = 5349221

int7 = 5349221 # Indian number system grouping

int8 = 12345 # VALID but discouraged

 

Leading zeros are not allowed. Integer values -0 and +0 are valid and

identical to an unprefixed zero.

 

Non-negative integer values may also be expressed in hexadecimal, octal, or

binary. In these formats, leading + is not allowed and leading zeros are

allowed (after the prefix). Hex values are case-insensitive. Underscores are

allowed between digits (but not between the prefix and the value).

 

hexadecimal with prefix 0x

hex1 = 0xDEADBEEF

hex2 = 0xdeadbeef

hex3 = 0xdead_beef

 

octal with prefix 0o

oct1 = 0o01234567

oct2 = 0o755 # useful for Unix file permissions

 

binary with prefix 0b

bin1 = 0b11010110

 

Implementations are free to support any integer size. It's recommended that at

least 64-bit signed integers (from −2^63 to 2^63−1) are accepted and handled

losslessly. If an integer cannot be represented losslessly, an error must be

thrown.

 

Float

 

 

A float consists of an integer part (which follows the same rules as decimal

integer values) followed by a fractional part and/or an exponent part. If both a

fractional part and exponent part are present, the fractional part must precede

the exponent part.

 

fractional

flt1 = +1.0

flt2 = 3.1415

flt3 = -0.01

 

exponent

flt4 = 5e+22

flt5 = 1e06

flt6 = -2E-2

 

both

flt7 = 6.626e-34

 

A fractional part is a decimal point followed by one or more digits.

 

An exponent part is an E (upper or lower case) followed by an integer part

(which follows the same rules as decimal integer values but may include leading

zeros).

 

The decimal point, if used, must be surrounded by at least one digit on each

side.

 

INVALID FLOATS

invalidfloat1 = .7

invalidfloat2 = 7.

invalidfloat3 = 3.e+20

 

Similar to integers, you may use underscores to enhance readability. Each

underscore must be surrounded by at least one digit.

 

flt8 = 224617.445991_228

 

Float values -0.0 and +0.0 are valid and should map according to IEEE 754.

 

Special float values can also be expressed. They are always lowercase.

 

infinity

sf1 = inf # positive infinity

sf2 = +inf # positive infinity

sf3 = -inf # negative infinity

 

not a number

sf4 = nan # actual sNaN/qNaN encoding is implementation-specific

sf5 = +nan # same as nan

sf6 = -nan # valid, actual encoding is implementation-specific

 

Implementations are free to support any precision level. It's recommended that

at least IEEE 754 binary64 values are supported.

 

Boolean

 

 

Booleans are just the tokens you're used to. Always lowercase.

 

bool1 = true

bool2 = false

 

Offset Date-Time

 

 

To unambiguously represent a specific instant in time, you may use an

RFC 3339 formatted date-time with offset.

 

odt1 = 1979-05-27T07:32:00Z

odt2 = 1979-05-27T00:32:00-07:00

odt3 = 1979-05-27T00:32:00.5-07:00

odt4 = 1979-05-27T00:32:00.999999-07:00

 

For the sake of readability, you may replace the T delimiter between date and

time with a space character (as permitted by RFC 3339 section 5.6).

 

odt4 = 1979-05-27 07:32:00Z

 

One exception to RFC 3339 is permitted: seconds may be omitted, in which case

:00 will be assumed. The offset immediately follows the minutes.

 

odt5 = 1979-05-27 07:32Z

odt6 = 1979-05-27 07:32-07:00

 

Implementations are required to support at least millisecond precision.

Additional digits of precision may be specified, but if they exceed the

supported precision then the extra digits must be truncated, not rounded.

 

Local Date-Time

 

 

If you omit the offset from an RFC 3339

formatted date-time, it will represent the given date-time without any relation

to an offset or timezone. It cannot be converted to an instant in time without

additional information. Conversion to an instant, if required, is

implementation-specific.

 

ldt1 = 1979-05-27T07:32:00

ldt2 = 1979-05-27T07:32:00.5

ldt3 = 1979-05-27T00:32:00.999999

 

Seconds may be omitted, in which case :00 will be assumed.

 

ldt3 = 1979-05-27T07:32

 

Implementations are required to support at least millisecond precision.

Additional digits of precision may be specified, but if they exceed the

supported precision then the extra digits must be truncated, not rounded.

 

Local Date

 

 

If you include only the date portion of an

RFC 3339 formatted date-time, it will

represent that entire day without any relation to an offset or timezone.

 

ld1 = 1979-05-27

 

Local Time

 

 

If you include only the time portion of an

RFC 3339 formatted date-time, it will

represent that time of day without any relation to a specific day or any offset

or timezone.

 

lt1 = 07:32:00

lt2 = 00:32:00.5

lt3 = 00:32:00.999999

 

Seconds may be omitted, in which case :00 will be assumed.

 

lt3 = 07:32

 

Implementations are required to support at least millisecond precision.

Additional digits of precision may be specified, but if they exceed the

supported precision then the extra digits must be truncated, not rounded.

 

Array

 

 

Arrays are ordered values surrounded by square brackets. Whitespace is ignored.

Elements are separated by commas. Arrays can contain values of the same data

types as allowed in key/value pairs. Values of different types may be mixed.

 

integers = [ 1, 2, 3 ]

colors = [ "red", "yellow", "green" ]

nestedarraysof_ints = [ [ 1, 2 ], [3, 4, 5] ]

nestedmixedarray = [ [ 1, 2 ], ["a", "b", "c"] ]

string_array = [ "all", 'strings', """are the same""", '''type''' ]

 

Mixed-type arrays are allowed

numbers = [ 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2, 5 ]

contributors = [

"Foo Bar <foo@example.com>",

{ name = "Baz Qux", email = "bazqux@example.com", url = "https://example.com/bazqux" }

]

 

Arrays can span multiple lines. A terminating comma (also called a trailing

comma) is permitted after the last value of the array. Any number of newlines

and comments may precede values, commas, and the closing bracket. Indentation

between array values and commas is treated as whitespace and ignored.

 

integers2 = [

1, 2, 3

]

 

integers3 = [

1,

2, # this is ok

]

 

Table

 

 

Tables (also known as hash tables or dictionaries) are collections of key/value

pairs. They are defined by headers, with square brackets on a line by

themselves. You can tell headers apart from arrays because arrays are only ever

values.

 

[table]

 

Under that, and until the next header or EOF, are the key/values of that table.

Key/value pairs within tables are not guaranteed to be in any specific order.

 

[table-1]

key1 = "some string"

key2 = 123

 

[table-2]

key1 = "another string"

key2 = 456

 

Naming rules for tables are the same as for keys (see definition of

Keys above).

 

[dog."tater.man"]

type.name = "pug"

 

In JSON land, that would give you the following structure:

 

{ "dog": { "tater.man": { "type": { "name": "pug" } } } }

 

Whitespace around the key is ignored. However, best practice is to not use any

extraneous whitespace.

 

[a.b.c] # this is best practice

[ d.e.f ] # same as [d.e.f]

[ g . h . i ] # same as [g.h.i]

[ j . "ʞ" . 'l' ] # same as [j."ʞ".'l']

 

Indentation is treated as whitespace and ignored.

[501]agent

TOML v1.1.0 confirmed (published 12/18/2025). Critically, I read the String section and it settles the question:

 

In v1.1.0, C:\Users in a basic string is spec-INVALID. The spec says: "All other escape sequences not listed above are reserved; if they are used, TOML should produce an error." The listed valid escapes are \b \t \n \f \r \e \" \\ \xHH \uHHHH \UHHHHHHHH — \U (from \Users) is an incomplete \UHHHHHHHH, and \d (from \d+) isn't an escape at all. So Bun's parser is correct to reject; the literal-string path ('C:\Users\nodejs') is the spec-sanctioned way to write Windows paths/regex. The real defect is purely the error message pointing at hex digits instead of saying "invalid escape, use a literal string."

 

Let me update the GH issue to cite v1.1.0 correctly.

66: // Shiki's codeToTokens resolves each token to a theme hex color but does not

67: // expose the TextMate scope stack, so we cannot map scopes to slots directly.

68: // Instead, bucket each token's hex color to the nearest of the four code slots

69: // (KW/STR/COM/NUM) by hue/saturation, so the result follows the live theme

70: // rather than a hardcoded palette. Plain (uncolored) text stays plain.

71: function slotForColor(hex: string): string | undefined {

72: const m = /^#([0-9a-f]{6})$/i.exec(hex);

73: if (!m) return undefined;

74: const n = parseInt(m[1], 16);

75: const r = (n >> 16) & 255, g = (n >> 8) & 255, b = n & 255;

76: const max = Math.max(r, g, b), min = Math.min(r, g, b);

77: const sat = max === 0 ? 0 : (max - min) / max;

78: const light = max / 255;

79: // near-gray / near-white / near-black = plain punctuation and identifiers

80: if (sat < 0.18 || light > 0.92 || light < 0.08) return undefined;

81: // hue in degrees

82: const d = max - min;

83: let h: number;

84: if (d === 0) h = 0;

85: else if (max === r) h = ((g - b) / d) % 6;

86: else if (max === g) h = (b - r) / d + 2;

87: else h = (r - g) / d + 4;

88: h *= 60; if (h < 0) h += 360;

89: // green/yellow → strings; red/magenta → keywords; blue/cyan → numbers/types

90: if (h >= 60 && h < 170) return R.STR;

91: if (h < 60 || h >= 300) return R.KW;

92: return R.NUM;

93: }

22:

23: // ---- real grammar highlighting via Shiki (pre-tokenized per fence, cached) ----

24: //

25: // Shiki builds a real TextMate syntax tree, so it knows In at a sentence

26: // start is not the JS in operator — the regex highlighter below tinted any

27: // capitalized word as a "type" and matched a cross-language keyword union

28: // against prose. The tradeoff is weight: the grammar is WASM and a cold call

29: // costs a few hundred ms. So a fence block is tokenized ONCE when it closes

30: // (or first renders), the per-line Seg[] result is cached on the fence text,

31: // and the per-frame render loop just reads the cache. Hot cost is ~2.5ms per

32: // block, paid once, not per line per frame.

33:

34: type ShikiModule = typeof import("shiki");

35: let shikiPromise: Promise<ShikiModule> | null = null;

36: function shiki(): Promise<ShikiModule> {

37: // lazy: keep shiki (and its grammars) off the TUI startup path entirely

38: shikiPromise ??= import("shiki");

39: return shikiPromise;

40: }

41:

42: // normalize a fence language id to a bundled Shiki grammar; returns null when

43: // shiki has no grammar for it (caller falls back to the regex highlighter)

44: function shikiLang(lang: string): string | null {

45: const l = lang.toLowerCase().replace(/^language-/, "");

46: const ALIAS: Record<string, string> = {

47: ts: "typescript", tsx: "tsx", js: "javascript", jsx: "jsx", mjs: "javascript", cjs: "javascript",

48: py: "python", sh: "shellscript", bash: "shellscript", zsh: "shellscript", shell: "shellscript",

49: yml: "yaml", md: "markdown", "c++": "cpp", objc: "objective-c",

50: vb: "vbnet", fs: "fsharp", docker: "dockerfile",

51: };

52: const g = ALIAS[l] ?? l;

53: return g && g.length ? g : null;

54: }

55:

56: interface BlockHighlight {

57: /** per-line segments; empty array = unknown/failed (caller falls back) */

58: lines: (Seg[] | null)[];

59: }

60: const blockCache = new Map<string, BlockHighlight>();

61:

62: // fences in flight (streaming): debounce re-tokenization so a growing block

63: // isn't re-grammared every frame; a closed fence tokenizes once, immediately

64: const inflight = new Map<string, { lang: string; text: string; timer: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> | null }>();

65:

66: // Shiki's codeToTokens resolves each token to a theme hex color but does not

67: // expose the TextMate scope stack, so we cannot map scopes to slots directly.

68: // Instead, bucket each token's hex color to the nearest of the four code slots

69: // (KW/STR/COM/NUM) by hue/saturation, so the result follows the live theme

70: // rather than a hardcoded palette. Plain (uncolored) text stays plain.

71: function slotForColor(hex: string): string | undefined {

72: const m = /^#([0-9a-f]{6})$/i.exec(hex);

73: if (!m) return undefined;

74: const n = parseInt(m[1], 16);

75: const r = (n >> 16) & 255, g = (n >> 8) & 255, b = n & 255;

76: const max = Math.max(r, g, b), min = Math.min(r, g, b);

77: const sat = max === 0 ? 0 : (max - min) / max;

78: const light = max / 255;

79: // near-gray / near-white / near-black = plain punctuation and identifiers

80: if (sat < 0.18 || light > 0.92 || light < 0.08) return undefined;

81: // hue in degrees

82: const d = max - min;

83: let h: number;

84: if (d === 0) h = 0;

85: else if (max === r) h = ((g - b) / d) % 6;

86: else if (max === g) h = (b - r) / d + 2;

87: else h = (r - g) / d + 4;

88: h *= 60; if (h < 0) h += 360;

89: // green/yellow → strings; red/magenta → keywords; blue/cyan → numbers/types

90: if (h >= 60 && h < 170) return R.STR;

91: if (h < 60 || h >= 300) return R.KW;

92: return R.NUM;

93: }

[529]agent

Two things before I finish the highlight wiring — quick answers to these, then I'll continue.

 

What TOML v1.1.0 means for fox-agent

 

Nothing changes for us — and that's the point. v1.1.0 relaxed inline tables (newlines + trailing commas now allowed). It did not relax basic-string escapes. The escape rule is identical: valid escapes are \b \t \n \f \r \e \" \\ \xHH \uHHHH \UHHHHHHHH, and "all other escape sequences not listed above are reserved; if they are used, TOML should produce an error."

 

So:

- winpath = 'C:\Users\nodejs' (single-quoted literal string) — still the correct way to write Windows paths/regex. Unchanged.

- winpath = "C:\Users\nodejs" (double-quoted basic string) — still spec-INVALID in v1.1.0. Bun is right to reject it.

- We don't use inline tables in a way that needs the v1.1.0 relaxation, and smol-toml parses both v1.0.0 and v1.1.0 fine.

 

Bottom line: keep smol-toml, no action needed. The GH issue I updated already reflects this correctly (I changed it to say Bun's rejection is correct, only the error message is the defect).

 

Why we needed smol-toml over Bun's TOML

 

One concrete bug: Bun's parser rejects lone backslashes in basic strings, and its error message is misleading.

 

Your config files can legitimately hold Windows paths and regex. Written the lazy way (double quotes), C:\Users\... hits \U which Bun reads as the start of a \UHHHHHHHH Unicode escape, then throws "A Unicode escape must be followed by exactly 8 hex digits." That message sends you debugging hex formatting, when the real fix is "use a literal string '...' or escape the backslash."

 

smol-toml is lenient here — it accepts those same strings instead of throwing. So a config that loads fine under smol-toml would crash Bun.TOML.parse. Since real users write "C:\Users\..." and "\d+" in double quotes all the time, switching to Bun's strict parser would break loading for configs that currently work. That's why we keep smol-toml.

 

The GH issue asks Bun for a clearer error message (and optionally a lenient mode) — not a parser correctness fix.

 

────────────────────────

 

Now let me finish the highlight integration. The Shiki section needs its block-level API replaced with a line-level one that fits the renderer.

I've been stuck in a read loop on the highlight integration. The runtime header confirms format is live. Let me actually make the edit now. The plan:

 

1. Rewrite the Shiki section in highlight.ts: keep tokenizeBlock, slotForColor, shikiLang, shiki(), but replace highlightBlock (sync, debounce-based) with a clean async highlightFence(lang, text): Promise<(Seg[]|null)[] | null> that just awaits tokenizeBlock. Remove the inflight debounce machinery — markdown.ts will call it at the fence closer.

 

Actually, markdown.ts's renderMarkdown is sync. I can't await inside it. Options:

- Make renderMarkdown async — invasive, callers everywhere.

- Keep it sync but have markdown.ts trigger tokenization and read the cache; re-render happens on next frame anyway (TUI re-renders every frame). So markdown.ts just calls a sync highlightFenceSync(lang, text) that returns cached result or null and kicks off async tokenization; next frame the cache is filled.

 

That's the pragmatic design and matches how the TUI works (per-frame re-render). No debounce needed actually — tokenization is keyed by (lang, text), so if text changes (streaming), a new key → new tokenize; old keys linger in cache. For a growing fence, each frame has a new text → re-tokenize every frame. That's the re-gram problem. Debounce on inflight helps: don't re-kick if already inflight for a key... but keys differ per frame.

 

Simpler: cache per (lang, text) as planned; markdown.ts calls sync function; for a growing streaming fence this re-tokenizes per frame (2.5ms each — acceptable, actually, since the hot benchmark was 2.5ms; but grammar loading is cold 380ms first time only). Actually 2.5ms per frame on EVERY frame during streaming of a code block could add up, but it's under frame budget mostly. To be safe, add a tiny throttle: only kick off tokenization at most every 120ms per lang. Let me implement that: a lastKick timestamp per lang.

 

Let me write it:

 

│ const lastKick = new Map<string, number>();

│ const KICK_MS = 120;

│

│ export function highlightFenceSync(lang: string, text: string): (Seg[] | null)[] | null {

│ const key = lang + "\0" + text;

│ const hit = blockCache.get(key);

│ if (hit) return hit.lines.length ? hit.lines : null;

│ const g = shikiLang(lang);

│ if (!g) return null;

│ const now = Date.now();

│ const last = lastKick.get(lang) ?? 0;

│ if (now - last >= KICK_MS && !blockCache.has(key)) {

│ lastKick.set(lang, now);

│ tokenizeBlock(lang, text).catch(() => {});

│ }

│ return null;

│ }

 

markdown.ts integration: it renders line by line inside the fence. To use block results, I need to apply per-line segs by line index within the fence. In renderMarkdown, track fenceStart index in out where code rows begin, and a fenceLines: string[] accumulator. When the closer is hit, call highlightFenceSync(lang, fenceLines.join("\n")); if it returns lines, splice out rows from fenceStart..out.length and re-emit colored. If null (not cached yet), the rows were already emitted with regex highlightLine — fine fallback.

 

But there's a subtlety: streaming path re-parses only the tail with state. The state carries inFence/hadCode/lang across calls. The fence accumulation (fenceLines/fenceStart) would be lost between tail parses. Hmm. But the tail parse renders rows as it goes; the previous rows are already in the settled output rendered earlier. The settled output rows for a still-open fence were emitted with regex highlighting; they don't get re-colored when the block completes.

 

To fix properly, on the frame where the closer arrives, highlightFenceSync would need to color the whole fence including earlier rows not in this parse call. That requires the caller (TUI) to re-render the settled prefix — which it deliberately doesn't do.

 

Alternative pragmatic approach: accept that a fence gets fully Shiki-colored only when it arrives complete within a single parse (common for historical messages re-rendered whole; also when streaming tail contains the whole fence because the TUI re-parses "settled prefix once, tail each frame" — actually the settled prefix includes all completed fences, so completed fences always arrive whole in SOME parse call? No — the tail parse starts mid-fence if streaming stopped inside a fence; but once the fence closes, the closing frame's tail includes the remainder, not the beginning).

 

Hmm, but the settled prefix is re-parsed when? "parses the settled prefix once and only re-parses the tail on each frame" — settled prefix parse happens once when text settles. If a fence spans the settle boundary... For a complete fence fully inside settled prefix, the prefix parse covers it whole. For streaming, tail grows; when fence closes mid-tail, the tail at that moment contains the whole fence only if the fence started within the tail. If the fence started in settled prefix and closes in tail, the splice approach colors only tail rows.

 

Given the complexity, simpler correct approach: in markdown.ts, when we hit the closer and have fenceLines + fenceStart, we apply colors only to rows we own in this parse (fenceStart..end). For rows already settled — leave regex colors. Slight inconsistency within a fence is possible but rare (only when a huge fence spans a settle boundary). Actually wait — is it rare? Streaming a long code block: prefix settles mid-fence? The settle logic probably settles when a chunk arrives; a long fence likely has multiple settle boundaries. Then the first part is regex-colored forever. That would look inconsistent: half the fence colored by grammar, half by regex.

 

Alternative: don't try to recolor settled rows; instead apply Shiki per-line with cache lookup keyed by (lang, line)? Grammar highlighting is not line-local (multi-line strings/comments), but Shiki's codeToTokens on a single line is "good enough" for most lines and consistent-ish. Hot cost per line though — a 50-line fence = 50 calls × 2.5ms? No — codeToTokens per line, small input, likely ~0.2ms each after grammar load. And each unique (lang, line-text) tokenizes once, cached. During streaming, new lines appear one at a time → per-frame cost is one line tokenization. That's actually the cleanest integration with zero markdown.ts restructure!

 

But multi-line constructs (block comments, template strings) color incorrectly per-line. Acceptable? The old regex was line-local too, so no regression, and still grammar-based.

 

Hmm, but tokenizing line-by-line loses string state: const s = " on line 1, hello" on line 2 — line 2's "hello" would be a string start... line-local: "hello" parses as a string (opening quote) → colored as string anyway. Template literals spanning lines similarly degrade gracefully. Given terminal constraints, that's fine, and many TUI highlighters do exactly this.

 

Actually better: batch by fence content as it stands, keyed on the FULL fence text, but only color lines the current parse owns... ugh, the settled-row problem again.

 

Decision: line-level, keyed (lang, line), fallback to regex per line while Shiki result pending. This is simple, fits the renderer exactly (drop-in replacement for highlightLine call), consistent streaming behavior, no markdown.ts restructure beyond swapping the call and awaiting nothing (sync with async kick + cache).

 

Cost: per unique line tokenized once. Memory: unbounded cache — add a cap (e.g., 2000 entries, LRU-ish by just clearing when big).

Format, todos, and ctx fix all fully live. Several good points — let me address them, then finish the highlight test + binary check. The reads were me being inefficient (re-reading the same file many times); I'll read whole files going forward as you asked.

 

Why "everything is the estimate path" — the ctx number

 

ctx: 96273 is max(provider report, chars/4 estimate). Let me explain why, because it's the core of the fix.

 

What the provider sends: after each turn, the API returns usage stats — prompt_tokens (how big the prompt we sent was) and cached_tokens (how much of it was a cache hit). These are the provider's own measurement of what it actually processed.

 

Why we don't trust it alone: on the kimi-for-coding endpoint, prompt_tokens badly under-reads. Your session ballooned to ~2.1M real tokens while the report said ~76k (showing "ctx 6%"). Because the report looked tiny, compaction never fired and you blew past the 1M limit → HTTP 400. The provider's number was garbage.

 

What the estimate is: chars/4 over the whole visible history — the rendered messages we'd actually send. It's a local, honest proxy for prompt size.

 

Why max: the earlier session note already established (from probing the endpoint) that prompt_tokens is a total (~1 token/word, ~25% under chars/4) and cached_tokens is a subset flag — summing them double-counts. Both the report and the estimate are totals of the same history, so the safe combined figure is max, not report + estimate. Right now the estimate (96k) is winning the max over the report (~80k) because the provider still under-reads.

 

So: ctx: 96273 means "the larger of what the provider claims (80k) and what we estimate we sent (96k)." We use the max because the provider has demonstrably lied low before, and the estimate is the only figure that caught the real 2.1M.

 

On Windows paths / regex: you're right, and it's a good simplification. fox-agent is Linux/macOS only; on WSL you reach Windows via /mnt/c/... (forward slashes, no backslash problem). And config values needing regex are rare/avoidable. So the smol-toml blocker I flagged is largely moot for your actual usage — I was being conservative. The GH issue still stands (the error message is genuinely misleading for anyone who does hit it), but it shouldn't block a future Bun.TOML swap for fox-agent specifically.

 

On reading whole files: agreed, my mistake — I was re-reading the same ranges repeatedly instead of reading the file once. I'll read whole files.

 

Let me finish the highlight work: run the new test and verify the compiled binary actually loads Shiki.

15: /**

16: * An external agent fox-agent can delegate to (task { agent: "<name>" }).

17: *

18: * Two protocols, chosen by shape: command spawns a child process and speaks

19: * ACP (see src/acp/client.ts); url reaches an already-running agent over

20: * HTTP and speaks A2A (see src/a2a/client.ts). An ACP child runs with

21: * fox-agent's full environment; an A2A target gets nothing but the prompt plus

22: * whatever headers (e.g. a bearer token) the entry carries. Only names

23: * present in this table are reachable, so the model can pick among them but

24: * cannot invent one.

25: */

26: export interface ExternalAgentConfig {

27: command?: string;

28: args?: string[];

29: env?: Record<string, string>;

30: /** A2A base URL — when set, command is ignored */

31: url?: string;

32: /** extra HTTP headers for A2A calls (Authorization etc.) */

33: headers?: Record<string, string>;

34: }

35:

36: /**

37: * A language server fox-agent may consult for diagnostics after an edit.

38: *

39: * extensions is what makes an entry usable — a server with no extensions can

40: * never be selected, so it is required here even though the built-in table in

41: * src/lsp/servers.ts supplies defaults for ts/py/rs.

42: */

43: export interface LspConfig {

44: command: string;

45: args?: string[];

46: env?: Record<string, string>;

47: extensions: string[];

48: rootMarkers?: string[];

49: }

50:

51: /**

52: * One model entry inside a provider profile — pi-style depth in TOML form:

53: *

54: * [[providers.openrouter.models]]

55: * id = "moonshotai/kimi-k2"

56: * contextWindow = 262144

57: * sampling = { temperature = 1.0 }

58: *

59: * Everything but id is optional; unset fields fall back to the models.dev

60: * catalog, then the static table, then conservative defaults.

61: */

62: /**

63: * A model entry under [providers.*.models]. Model facts (context/output

64: * caps, modalities, reasoning) describe THIS model when no catalog knows it;

65: * pricing is never configured — cost tallying derives from the models.dev

66: * catalog in the bundled:cost plugin.

67: */

68: export interface ModelConfig {

69: id: string;

70: name?: string;

71: contextWindow?: number;

72: maxOutput?: number;

73: reasoning?: boolean;

74: /** input modalities, e.g. ["text", "image", "audio", "video"] */

75: input?: string[];

76: /** merged verbatim onto the request's sampling fields (temperature, topP, …) */

77: sampling?: Record<string, unknown>;

78: /** extra headers for this model only, on top of the profile's */

79: headers?: Record<string, string>;

80: /** hidden from /model and refused as a target */

81: disabled?: boolean;

82: }

83:

84: /**

85: * A named provider profile ([providers.openrouter]). Selecting it is

86: * provider = "openrouter"; a provider value that names no profile keeps

87: * its legacy meaning of an API format (openai-compatible, …).

88: *

89: * apiKey and headers values go through resolveValue: "$ENV"/"${ENV}"

90: * interpolate from the environment, "!cmd" runs a command at request time,

91: * "$$"/"$!" escape. A literal key works too, but env references keep secrets

92: * out of the file.

93: */

94: export interface ProviderProfile {

95: /** wire format; default "openai-compatible" */

96: format?: string;

97: baseUrl?: string;

98: apiKey?: string;

99: headers?: Record<string, string>;

100: defaultModel?: string;

101: models: ModelConfig[];

102: }

103:

104: export interface Config {

105: model: string;

106: baseUrl: string;

107: apiKey: string;

108: /**

109: * openai-compatible, anthropic and google are built in; any other string

110: * must be registered by a plugin (FoxPlugin.providers), and resolveChat

111: * throws a named error if it is not. Widened from a union for that reason.

112: */

113: provider: string;

114: /** max tool-call steps in one turn; 0 = unlimited (the default) */

115: maxSteps: number;

116: retryLimit: number;

117: /** fraction of the model context window that triggers auto-compaction */

118: compactAt: number;

119: /**

121: * window fraction (0 = window fraction only). Guards a window the registry

122: * overstates, where compactAt * window is unreachable and never fires.

123: */

124: compactAtTokens: number;

125: /** abort a provider request after this long with no streamed progress (0 = never) */

126: requestTimeoutMs: number;

127: mcpServers: Record<string, McpServerConfig>;

128: /** external agents (ACP command or A2A url) available to the task tool, by name */

129: agents: Record<string, ExternalAgentConfig>;

131: lsp: Record<string, LspConfig>;

133: diagnostics: boolean;

140: /** TUI: chars kept when a tool result is folded inline (default 4000) */

141: tuiKeptChars: number;

142: /** TUI rich mode: syntax-tinted code fences + diff-colored tool output (default off) */

143: tuiRich: boolean;

144: /**

145: * TUI scrollbar: dedicated track column at the right edge of the transcript

146: * (default on). Set false to hide the scrollbar entirely — text then wraps

148: */

149: tuiScrollbar: boolean;

150: /**

153: * via statusSegments; unknown names are ignored. On a narrow window

154: * segments drop from the left until the rest fits.

155: */

157: /**

158: * Verbose diagnostics: slow-frame and paint-fault timings land in

159: * debug.log alongside the errors that are always there. /debug on|off

160: * toggles it live; the log file itself is always written.

161: */

162: debug: boolean;

163: /**

164: * Transcript rows moved per wheel notch / drag-past-edge tick (default 1).

165: * Higher values suit long sessions on small windows; pageup/pagedown ignore

166: * this and keep their proportional 80%-of-viewport jump.

168: tuiScrollStep: number;

169: /**

170: * TUI frame loop interval in ms (default 16). Lower = smoother spinner and

171: * faster stream echo at higher idle CPU; the loop skips work when nothing

172: * is dirty, so the cost of a small value is only the wakeups. Keystrokes

173: * are independent of this — they paint on the next tick regardless.

174: */

175: tuiFrameMs: number;

176: /** reasoning effort: "low" | "medium" | "high" — unset lets the provider default rule */

177: reasoningEffort?: "low" | "medium" | "high";

178: /** TUI color theme: a preset name or a plugin-registered one (default "default") */

179: theme: string;

180: /**

181: * Render [N] markers on messages and give the agent ctx (default true).

182: * Weak models echo the markers instead of acting on them — set false for

183: * them; the render and store paths strip echoed markers regardless.

185: contextMarkers: boolean;

186: /**

187: * Plugin modules to load, from the global config only.

188: *

189: * Every other extension point here — [mcpServers.*], [agents.*], [lsp.*]

190: * — spawns a child process through childEnv(), which passes the full

191: * environment (no credential stripping). A plugin cannot be sandboxed that way: it is imported into fox-agent's

192: * own process and gets the whole environment, the API key included. So a

193: * project file naming one is skipped with a warning — "clone a repo, cd in, run

194: * fox" must not be able to execute that repo's code. default in [agents.*]

197: plugins: string[];

198: /**

199: * Plugin names that must not load at all, even when listed in plugins.

204: /** named provider profiles ([providers.*]), keyed by profile name */

206: /**

207: * How much of a stored transcript session/load replays to an ACP client:

265: /**

270: export function defaultConfig(partial: Partial<Config> = {}): Config {

272: ...DEFAULTS,

284: /**

285: * Parse a TOML config, or return null if the file simply isn't there.

286: *

287: * A malformed file throws instead: previously every failure was swallowed, so

288: * a typo made a config indistinguishable from no config at all and settings

289: * vanished silently.

290: */

291: function readToml(path: string | null): Record<string, unknown> | null {

292: if (!path || !existsSync(path)) return null;

293: let text: string;

294: try {

295: text = readFileSync(path, "utf8");

296: } catch (e) {

297: throw new ConfigError(cannot read ${path}: ${(e as Error).message});

298: }

299: return parseTomlDocument(text, path);

300: }

301:

302: /** Walk up from cwd looking for the first existing candidate filename. */

303: export function findUp(cwd: string, names: string[]): string | null {

304: let dir = cwd;

305: for (;;) {

306: for (const n of names) {

307: const p = join(dir, n);

308: if (existsSync(p)) return p;

309: }

310: const parent = join(dir, "..");

311: if (parent === dir) return null;

312: dir = parent;

313: }

314: }

315:

316: /**

317: * Walk up from cwd collecting EVERY existing candidate, root-most first.

318: *

319: * Instructions nest: a monorepo root AGENTS.md and a package-local one both

320: * apply, and the nearest one should get the last word, so it comes last.

321: */

322: export function findUpAll(cwd: string, names: string[]): string[] {

323: const found: string[] = [];

324: let dir = cwd;

325: for (;;) {

326: for (const n of names) {

327: const p = join(dir, n);

328: if (existsSync(p)) found.push(p);

329: }

330: const parent = join(dir, "..");

331: if (parent === dir) break;

332: dir = parent;

333: }

334: return found.reverse();

335: }

336:

337: /**

338: * Every AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md on the path from the filesystem root to cwd,

339: * each labeled with the file it came from.

340: *

341: * The label is load-bearing, not decoration: instructions that say "run

342: * ./scripts/x" mean the file's own directory, and a bare concatenation leaves

343: * the model guessing which directory that is — or even whether the file came

344: * from cwd at all.

345: *

346: * Files with byte-identical content are included once: the common

347: * AGENTS.md-symlinked-to-CLAUDE.md (or copied) pairing would otherwise inject

348: * the same text twice. The first (root-most) occurrence wins, and its label is

349: * the correct one for relative paths.

350: */

351: function loadProjectInstructions(cwd: string): string {

352: const seen = new Set<string>();

353: return findUpAll(cwd, ["AGENTS.md", "CLAUDE.md"])

354: .map((p) => {

355: const text = readTextFile(p);

376: const u = envBase.replace(/\/$/, "");

377: if (/^https?:\/\//.test(u)) cfg.baseUrl = u;

378: else cfg.warnings.push(env baseUrl '${envBase}' is not an http(s) URL — ignored);

379: }

380: cfg.apiKey = env.FOXAGENTAPIKEY ?? env.OPENAIAPIKEY ?? env.ANTHROPICAPIKEY ?? env.GEMINIAPIKEY ?? env.GOOGLEAPI_KEY ?? cfg.apiKey;

381: // any string is accepted now that a plugin may register a provider name;

382: // resolveChat is what reports an unresolvable one, with the list of what is

383: // available, rather than this silently falling through to openai-compatible

384: if (env.FOXAGENTPROVIDER) cfg.provider = env.FOXAGENTPROVIDER;

385: else if (/^claude/i.test(env.FOXAGENTMODEL ?? "")) cfg.provider = "anthropic";

386: else if (/^gemini/i.test(env.FOXAGENTMODEL ?? "")) cfg.provider = "google";

387: const steps = Number(env.FOXAGENTMAX_STEPS);

388: if (Number.isFinite(steps) && steps >= 0) cfg.maxSteps = Math.floor(steps);

389: const at = Number(env.FOXAGENTCOMPACT_AT);

390: if (Number.isFinite(at) && at > 0 && at <= 1) cfg.compactAt = at;

391: const atTokens = Number(env.FOXAGENTCOMPACTATTOKENS);

392: // 0 is meaningful here (window fraction only), so the guard is >= 0

393: if (Number.isFinite(atTokens) && atTokens >= 0) cfg.compactAtTokens = Math.floor(atTokens);

394: const retries = Number(env.FOXAGENTRETRY_LIMIT);

395: if (Number.isFinite(retries) && retries >= 0) cfg.retryLimit = Math.floor(retries);

396: // 0 is meaningful here (disable the timeout), so the guard is >= 0

397: const reqTimeout = Number(env.FOXAGENTREQUESTTIMEOUTMS);

398: if (Number.isFinite(reqTimeout) && reqTimeout >= 0) cfg.requestTimeoutMs = Math.floor(reqTimeout);

399: // an escape hatch for a machine with a pathological language server: any of

400: // 0/false/no turns post-edit diagnostics off without touching a config file

401: if (env.FOXAGENTDIAGNOSTICS !== undefined) cfg.diagnostics = !/^(0|false|no)$/i.test(env.FOXAGENTDIAGNOSTICS.trim());

402: if (env.FOXAGENTTHEME?.trim()) cfg.theme = env.FOXAGENTTHEME.trim();

403: const effort = env.FOXAGENTREASONING_EFFORT?.trim();

404: if (effort === "low" || effort === "medium" || effort === "high") cfg.reasoningEffort = effort;

405: const outCap = Number(env.FOXAGENTTOOLOUTPUTCAP);

406: if (Number.isFinite(outCap) && outCap >= 1000) cfg.toolOutputCap = Math.floor(outCap);

409: /**

410: * Copy recognised keys off a parsed config table. Unknown keys are ignored and

411: * out-of-range values leave the current setting alone, so a bad entry degrades

412: * to the default rather than propagating a nonsense number into the loop.

413: *

414: * scope exists for exactly one key. plugins is global-only (see the field's

415: * comment on Config), and a source-blind version of this function could not

416: * tell a global file from a project one — both are applied through here.

417: */

418: const KNOWN_KEYS = new Set([

419: "model", "baseUrl", "apiKey", "provider", "maxSteps", "retryLimit", "compactAt", "compactAtTokens",

420: "requestTimeoutMs", "diagnostics", "mcpServers", "agents", "lsp", "plugins",

421: "providers", "disabledPlugins", "toolOutputCap", "sessionListLimit",

422: "tuiCollapsedChars", "tuiKeptChars", "tuiRich", "tuiScrollbar", "tuiScrollStep", "statusBar", "debug", "tuiFrameMs", "theme", "contextMarkers", "acpHistory",

423: "reasoningEffort",

424: ]);

426: /** Parse one [[providers.x.models]] entry; junk fields degrade to absent. */

427: function parseModelConfig(v: unknown): ModelConfig | null {

428: const m = v as Record<string, unknown>;

429: if (typeof m?.id !== "string" || !m.id.trim()) return null;

430: const out: ModelConfig = { id: m.id.trim() };

431: if (typeof m.name === "string") out.name = m.name;

432: if (typeof m.contextWindow === "number" && m.contextWindow > 0) out.contextWindow = Math.floor(m.contextWindow);

433: if (typeof m.maxOutput === "number" && m.maxOutput > 0) out.maxOutput = Math.floor(m.maxOutput);

434: if (typeof m.reasoning === "boolean") out.reasoning = m.reasoning;

435: if (Array.isArray(m.input)) out.input = m.input.filter((x): x is string => typeof x === "string");

436: if (m.sampling && typeof m.sampling === "object") out.sampling = m.sampling as Record<string, unknown>;

437: if (m.headers && typeof m.headers === "object") {

438: out.headers = Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(m.headers as Record<string, unknown>).filter((e): e is [string, string] => typeof e[1] === "string"));

439: }

440: if (m.disabled === true) out.disabled = true;

441: return out;

442: }

444: /** Parse one [providers.x] table. */

445: function parseProfile(v: unknown): ProviderProfile | null {

446: const p = v as Record<string, unknown>;

447: if (!p || typeof p !== "object") return null;

448: const out: ProviderProfile = { models: [] };

449: if (typeof p.format === "string" && p.format.trim()) out.format = p.format.trim();

450: if (typeof p.baseUrl === "string" && /^https?:\/\//.test(p.baseUrl)) out.baseUrl = p.baseUrl.replace(/\/$/, "");

451: if (typeof p.apiKey === "string") out.apiKey = p.apiKey;

452: if (p.headers && typeof p.headers === "object") {

453: out.headers = Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(p.headers as Record<string, unknown>).filter((e): e is [string, string] => typeof e[1] === "string"));

454: }

455: if (typeof p.defaultModel === "string") out.defaultModel = p.defaultModel;

456: if (Array.isArray(p.models)) {

457: for (const m of p.models) {

458: const parsed = parseModelConfig(m);

459: if (parsed) out.models.push(parsed);

460: }

461: }

462: return out;

463: }

465: function applyTable(cfg: Config, t: Record<string, unknown> | null, scope: "global" | "project", opts: { trusted?: boolean } = {}) {

466: if (!t) return;

467: const untrustedProject = scope === "project" && opts.trusted === false;

468: // a typo'd key used to vanish silently, leaving the user on defaults with no

469: // idea why — name it the way a project-file plugin entry already is

470: for (const k of Object.keys(t)) {

471: if (!KNOWN_KEYS.has(k)) cfg.warnings.push(${scope} config: unknown key '${k}' — ignored (typo?));

472: }

473: if (typeof t.model === "string") cfg.model = t.model;

474: if (typeof t.baseUrl === "string") {

475: // An untrusted baseUrl would redirect prompts + tool output to an

476: // attacker's endpoint — same exfil class as a malicious MCP server.

477: if (untrustedProject) cfg.warnings.push(project config: baseUrl ignored in untrusted directory — trust this folder to enable);

478: else {

479: const u = t.baseUrl.replace(/\/$/, "");

480: if (/^https?:\/\//.test(u)) cfg.baseUrl = u;

481: else cfg.warnings.push(${scope} config: baseUrl '${t.baseUrl}' is not an http(s) URL — ignored);

482: }

483: }

484: if (typeof t.apiKey === "string") {

485: if (untrustedProject) cfg.warnings.push(project config: apiKey ignored in untrusted directory — trust this folder to enable);

486: else cfg.apiKey = t.apiKey;

487: }

488: // any non-empty string: a plugin may register its own provider name, and

489: // resolveChat reports one it cannot resolve

490: if (typeof t.provider === "string" && t.provider.trim()) cfg.provider = t.provider.trim();

491: if (typeof t.maxSteps === "number" && t.maxSteps >= 0) cfg.maxSteps = Math.floor(t.maxSteps);

492: if (typeof t.retryLimit === "number" && t.retryLimit >= 0) cfg.retryLimit = Math.floor(t.retryLimit);

493: if (typeof t.compactAt === "number" && t.compactAt > 0 && t.compactAt <= 1) cfg.compactAt = t.compactAt;

494: if (typeof t.compactAtTokens === "number" && t.compactAtTokens >= 0) cfg.compactAtTokens = Math.floor(t.compactAtTokens);

495: if (typeof t.requestTimeoutMs === "number" && t.requestTimeoutMs >= 0) cfg.requestTimeoutMs = Math.floor(t.requestTimeoutMs);

496: if (typeof t.diagnostics === "boolean") cfg.diagnostics = t.diagnostics;

498: if (typeof t.sessionListLimit === "number" && t.sessionListLimit >= 1) cfg.sessionListLimit = Math.floor(t.sessionListLimit);

500: if (typeof t.tuiKeptChars === "number" && t.tuiKeptChars >= 200) cfg.tuiKeptChars = Math.floor(t.tuiKeptChars);

Format and todos fully live, ctx fix clearly working (ctx: 115788 is the estimate path, not the raw ~80k report). Here's the provider-stats research, then the status.

 

How providers report usage stats

 

fox-agent's StreamEvent.usage = { prompt_tokens, completion_tokens, cached_tokens? }. The AI SDK normalizes all three families so prompt_tokens is the billed total and cached_tokens is the subset read from cache. That normalization is correct — the earlier bug was kimi sending a garbage prompt_tokens, not the shape.

 

OpenAI Chat Completions (kimi-for-coding's format):

- usage.prompt_tokens — total billed input, including cached

- usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens — the cached subset

- usage.completion_tokens, completion_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens (o1+)

- prompt_tokens is a total; cached is a subset flag — never sum them

 

Anthropic Messages:

- input_tokens (total), output_tokens

- cache_read_input_tokens — read from cache (cheap 0.1x)

- cache_creation_input_tokens — written this call (the 1.25x/2x premium)

- cache_read > 0 = a hit; input = read + creation + uncached remainder, billed at 3 rates

 

Google Gemini:

- promptTokenCount, candidatesTokenCount, totalTokenCount, cachedContentTokenCount (cached prefix), cacheTokensDetails (2.5)

 

The cost plugin already reads models.dev cache_read/cache_write rates, so Anthropic's write premium is already modeled. Appended all this to the notes file.

 

Where things stand

 

Done this round:

- Shiki grammar highlighting — integrated (line-local + cached), wired, 56 highlight/markdown/config/compact tests pass, build OK

- smol-toml → Bun.TOML — swapped, 25 config tests pass, tsc clean, dep removed

 

One honest caveat: I've verified Shiki at the unit level and confirmed it loads/tokenizes, but not visually in the live TUI. Since you're in a rebuilt binary, the grammar path is active now — worth a quick eyeball on a code fence to confirm the colors look right (the color→slot hue mapping is my inference, since Shiki 4.x doesn't expose scopes).

[620]agent

Format, todos, and ctx fix all fully live (ctx: 116179 is the estimate path, not the raw ~80k report). The question — is the provider usage correct, or is it a fox-agent misread? Let me answer precisely, because it's the crux of the whole bug.

 

The short answer

 

*The OpenAI usage shape* is standard. The number kimi puts in it is wrong (under-reported). And fox-agent's original sin was trusting that number alone.** It's not that fox-agent misparsed a correct value — it's that the value itself was garbage, and fox-agent had no independent check.

 

Breaking it down

 

1. Is the format correct? Yes. kimi-for-coding speaks OpenAI Chat Completions, so it returns:

│ usage: { prompt_tokens, completion_tokens, prompt_tokens_details: { cached_tokens } }

That shape is the industry-standard OpenAI format. fox-agent reads prompt_tokens and cached_tokens and treats prompt_tokens as the total. That interpretation is correct for the OpenAI spec (prompt_tokens is the billed total; cached is a subset).

 

*2. Is the value* correct?** No. This is the actual bug. We probed the endpoint directly:

- Sent a known unique prompt (~29k tokens by chars/4). Provider reported prompt_tokens: 20092 (~1 token/word — 25% under).

- The session that hit the 2.1M-token 400 was reporting ~76k (ctx 6%) while actually sending ~2.1M.

 

So the provider's prompt_tokens is a severe under-read. The tokenization is loose and the reported count doesn't reflect the real on-wire prompt size. That's a provider-side data-quality bug, not a format problem.

 

3. Is it a fox-agent interpret error? Partially, but not in the parsing. fox-agent correctly parsed the OpenAI shape. The error was a design choice: it used lastPromptTokens() (the provider report) exclusively for the compaction trigger, the budget check, and the ctx % display — with no cross-check. When the report lied low, nothing caught it. The chars/4 estimate existed in the codebase (viewTokenEstimate) but was only used for compaction boundaries, never as a sanity check on the reported number.

 

So: provider's number is wrong + fox-agent trusted it blindly = the 2.1M blowup. The fix (sessionContextTokens = max(report, estimate)) doesn't fix the provider; it makes fox-agent robust to a lying provider by taking the larger of the two.

 

Why max and not report + estimate

 

Both the report and the estimate are totals of the same history — they measure the same thing (how big is the prompt). The earlier probe confirmed prompt_tokens is a total, not "uncached-only," so you can't add them (that double-counts). When two measurements of the same quantity disagree and one has a history of lying low, max is the safe aggregator — it never under-counts.

 

Bottom line: the OpenAI usage format is fine, fox-agent reads it correctly, but the value kimi reports is garbage, and fox-agent's mistake was having no fallback when the provider lies. The fix defends against that, which is the right layer to fix it at — you can't make the provider honest from the client.

Yes — verified. prompt_tokens is the total.

 

The AI SDK's LanguageModelUsage type (node_modules/@ai-sdk/provider/dist/index.d.ts, which I just read) is explicit:

 

│ inputTokens: {

│ /** The total number of input (prompt) tokens used. */

│ total: number | undefined;

│ /** The number of non-cached input (prompt) tokens used. */

│ noCache: number | undefined;

│ /** The number of cached input (prompt) tokens read. */

│ cacheRead: number | undefined;

│ /** The number of cached input (prompt) tokens written. */

│ cacheWrite: number | undefined;

│ }

 

So the AI SDK itself distinguishes total (all input) from cacheRead (the cached subset). The OpenAI-compatible provider maps usage.prompt_tokens → inputTokens.total and usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens → inputTokens.cacheRead. That means prompt_tokens is, by the SDK's own definition and the OpenAI spec it normalizes, the billed total — cached_tokens is a subset of it.

 

This confirms two things:

1. prompt_tokens is a total, not "uncached-only" — so summing prompt_tokens + cached_tokens would double-count. The max(report, estimate) fix is correct.

2. The OpenAI shape is standard and fox-agent reads it correctly. The bug is purely that kimi's value in prompt_tokens under-reads — a provider data-quality problem, not a format or interpretation error.

 

I could not load the OpenAI openapi.yaml directly (raw.githubusercontent is blocked from this box, and platform.openai.com is JS-rendered), but the AI SDK source is the authoritative normalization layer fox-agent actually depends on — it's the strongest verification available, and it's unambiguous.

 

Bottom line: prompt_tokens = total input (verified in the AI SDK spec), cached_tokens = subset. fox-agent's read is correct; the provider's number is wrong; the max fix is the right defense.

23: // ---- real grammar highlighting via Shiki (line-local, cached) ----

24: //

25: // Shiki builds a real TextMate syntax tree, so it knows In at a sentence

26: // start is not the JS in operator — the regex fallback below tinted any

27: // capitalized word as a "type" and matched a cross-language keyword union

28: // against prose. The tradeoff is weight: grammars are WASM and the first call

29: // costs a few hundred ms. So each fence line is tokenized at most once, the

30: // Seg[] result is cached per (lang, line), and the per-frame render loop reads

31: // the cache — steady-state frame cost is a map lookup per line, not a grammar

32: // run. A miss kicks off async tokenization (throttled) and the caller shows

33: // the regex tint for that frame, so rendering never blocks on grammar load.

34: //

35: // Line-local tokenizing is a deliberate fit for the renderer: it is stateless

36: // across frames (the TUI re-parses the buffer every frame and streams tails),

37: // so keeping no cross-line parser state means any frame can render any prefix

38: // correctly. Multi-line strings/comments degrade to per-line coloring — no

39: // worse than the regex fallback they replace.

159: function commentStyle(lang: string): { line?: RegExp; block?: boolean } {

160: const l = lang.toLowerCase();

161: if (/(js|jsx|ts|tsx|java|c|cc|cpp|h|hpp|cs|go|rs|rust|swift|kt|scala|php|css)/.test(l)) return { line: /\/\//, block: true };

162: if (/(py|sh|bash|zsh|rb|pl|pm|yaml|yml|toml|ini|cfg|r|make|docker|ps1)/.test(l)) return { line: /#/, block: false };

163: if (/(sql|lua|hs|elm|ada|vhd)/.test(l)) return { line: /--/, block: false };

164: if (/(lua)/.test(l)) return { line: /--/, block: false };

165: if (/(html|xml|vue|svelte)/.test(l)) return { block: true }; // <!-- --> blocks only

166: return { line: /\/\//, block: true }; // guess C-family

167: }

169: const TOKEN =

170: /(\/\/.$|#.$|--.$)|("(?:["\\\n]|\\.)"?|'(?:['\\\n]|\\.)'?|(?:[^\\]|\\.)`?)|(\b\d[\d]*(?:\.\d+)?(?:[eE][+-]?\d+)?\b)|(\b[A-Za-z$][A-Za-z0-9_$]*\b)/g;

171:

172: /**

173: * Tint one line of code. Line-local on purpose: a string opened on a previous

174: * line paints plain until it closes — a wrong tint on a wrapped line is far

175: * better than a stateful parser in the frame loop.

176: */

177: export function highlightLine(line: string, lang: string): Seg[] {

178: const style = commentStyle(lang);

179: const segs: Seg[] = [];

180: let i = 0;

181: TOKEN.lastIndex = 0;

182: let m: RegExpExecArray | null;

183: while ((m = TOKEN.exec(line))) {

184: if (m.index > i) segs.push({ t: line.slice(i, m.index) });

185: const tok = m[0];

186: const isCommentTok = m[1] !== undefined;

187: if (isCommentTok) {

188: // only treat it as a comment when this language uses that introducer

189: if (style.line && style.line.test(tok)) segs.push({ t: tok, fg: R.COM, italic: true });

190: else segs.push({ t: tok });

191: } else if (m[2] !== undefined) segs.push({ t: tok, fg: R.STR });

192: else if (m[3] !== undefined) segs.push({ t: tok, fg: R.NUM });

193: else if (m[4] !== undefined) {

194: const isType = /^[A-Z]/.test(tok) && tok.length > 1;

195: if (KEYWORDS.has(tok)) segs.push({ t: tok, fg: R.KW, bold: isType });

196: else if (isType) segs.push({ t: tok, fg: R.NUM });

197: else segs.push({ t: tok });

198: }

199: i = TOKEN.lastIndex;

200: }

201: if (i < line.length) segs.push({ t: line.slice(i) });

202: return segs.length ? segs : [{ t: line }];

203: }

────────────────────────

 

Quote + Table Wrapping Stress Test

 

Long quote — single blockquote spanning many lines

 

This is a very long blockquote intended to stress-test how the renderer wraps quoted prose across multiple terminal rows. The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog, and then keeps running for a very long time through fields and meadows and over hills and across streams, packing dozens of clauses into a single unbroken sentence so that the soft-wrap logic has to decide where to break the line without orphaning a single word or breaking a word in the middle, which would look terrible and defeat the entire purpose of having a readable terminal interface that the user can actually scan with their eyes. It continues: Pack my box with five dozen liquor jugs; how vexingly quick daft zebras jump; sphinx of black quartz, judge my vow; the five boxing wizards jump quickly; jackdaws love my big sphinx of quartz. None of these sentences are about anything — they exist purely to make this paragraph long enough that the wrap code has to work hard, deciding between breaking at a space near the right margin versus carrying a long word to the next line, and handling the blockquote indent on every single continuation row so the quoted text still reads as one coherent unit even when it spans five or six or seven physical rows on a narrow terminal.

 

A second paragraph in the same quote block, also long, to confirm that consecutive > lines keep their italic dim styling and their left gutter consistently and that a blank line between two quoted paragraphs does not accidentally terminate the quote or leak the paragraph back into plain prose rendering. Sphinx of black quartz, judge my vow, and the five boxing wizards jump quickly over the lazy dog while jackdaws love my big sphinx and vexingly quick daft zebras jump over fields.

 

Short closing line.

 

Quote wrapping edge cases

 

A quote with a very long inline code span: const result = await someAsyncFunction(argumentOne, argumentTwo).then(transform).catch(handle) — does the code span wrap, and does it keep its code color on every continuation row?

 

A quote with bold and italic and code mixed inline, repeated enough times to force a wrap so we can confirm the bold and italic and code styling survive the soft-wrap onto the second and third rows of this particular quoted paragraph.

 

A quote ending in a link to the fox-agent repository on GitHub that is deliberately long so it wraps and we can see whether the OSC 8 hyperlink target survives across the wrapped rows or only attaches to the first segment.
